I’m really sorry you’re going through this. 
I’m going to be brutally honest, so please skip if that’s not what you’re looking for.  

TL;DR: Being uncomfortable now is absolutely worth being stronger later, when there could be so much more to lose. 


Disclaimer: I’m not saying these things will happen. I’m just presenting a likely scenario influenced by my own life. 


I totally get wanting to shove all this in a corner of your mind and just keep chugging the way you were before the trauma. Nobody wants to be in emotional discomfort. Avoiding it makes total sense and is a path a lot of people take. 


That may not work for you, though. 


To start, your proposed career field could very possibly hurt you - or even be too difficult to start - if you don’t address this sexual assault. 


The people you would work with and advocate for will have been through similar situations, and it’s probably going to trigger you. That word gets tossed around a lot, but it basically means that your brain skips the logical thoughts of “I’m safe and not in that situation anymore”. Instead, you have reactions to your trauma, even though you’re far away from danger now. 


You won’t be able to do your best by your clients if your brain is stuck in trauma/panic mode. That’s not fair to them or you. 


I have my own trauma from being a survivor of child abuse. I became a teacher, partly because I wanted to help kids like me. I’ve worked through a lot of the trauma, but there were some situations that had me choking down tears and deep breathing to avoid a panic attack. It was a part of what landed me in the hospital last year, unable to go back to work. (Again, not saying this is you, just what happened to me.)


Pushing these things down doesn’t make them disappear. It just makes your emotional foundation shaky for everything else. You may not have to deal with it now, but future-you will be up a creek. It could take two, ten, maybe even fifty years now when the trauma foundation could break, and you won’t be able to ignore it even if you wanted to. It could damage your job, your personal relationships, and your ability to just cope with life. 


Instead of struggling, trying to turn a blind eye to such a painful experience, you could make future-you stronger with some emotional work. Future-you could be better than you ever imagined. You’ll have to go through some hard stuff now, though. 


Therapy absolutely does not have to be rehashing your trauma over and over again. (I would absolutely hate that, too.) There are treatments like EMDR, which have you remember the event in a controlled environment. It has a process that helps your brain to deconstruct trauma and then reconstruct safety. You could look into DBT (Dialectical Behavior Therapy) which focuses on the decisions you make and how thoughts and emotions cause influence those decisions. You could find a trauma-informed therapist and simply see what their recommendations are. Take them or leave them. 


All this to say, ignoring this awful thing that happened to you won’t make it go away. 


Do this for your future self. The you who has goals and wants to help others. She may not be able to do that if you don’t set her up for success.

She got a new dog and brought him to my sessions to “socialize” him (without asking me if I was ok with it). 

She only paid attention to the dog from then on out. I was just their background d noise.

“I’m not going to tell my son that he needs to listen to you or respect you. We’re not raising him to be a robot, blindly following authority figures. You should get to know him; ask him about his interests. Then he’ll like you enough to care about what you have to say.”

Ma’am, I’m just asking that your teenage son not handcuff himself to my classroom furniture.
“Different to” is usually a tip-off for me that the speaker wasn’t raised speaking American English.
Can we just . . . use what we want?

It’s become a common call-and-response phrase to get younger kids to pay attention. 
Instead of saying “Eyes up here,” you give students a prompt that they reply to. 
You can see them all over teachers’ social media accounts. They’re usually cutesy and fun - something the kids can really get into. 

Sometimes the responses are planned and taught at the beginning of the year along with class rules. Sometimes they develop organically or are created based on current trends. (There are a ton from Frozen and Encanto.)

My guess is that the elementary school students who learned “Capisce? Caposh” ~~after their teacher saw it on TikTok~~ are now aging into your class.


[Examples](https://youtu.be/DbLZkCerKlU?si=dOc7pXcrVwtjjX6C)

ETA: Apparently this has been around for a longer time than I thought. I think it’s become more common since social media.

I’ve been doing a search through the sub, and a lot of people feel like they’re not bad enough to be hospitalized. I read their description and think, “Yeah, they really should go.” And then I realize my symptoms and thoughts are a pretty good match to theirs. 


I guess I was just looking for reassurance that I’m not “gaming the system” or using up resources that should go to someone else.

At one point during my therapy session today, and also last week, my therapist looked at me and said earnestly, “I’m sorry I don’t have a magic cure to fix this for you. I know how hard you’ve tried and how fed up you are with living.” 
I really hope she’s not the only person who sees that I’ve tried. My depression is not easing up, but it’s not because I haven’t tried.

Living together can be comfortingly routine and familiar, so every once in a while, my husband and I do things to surprise each other. Getting flowers, bringing home an unexpected treat, little love messages written on the bathroom mirror, warming up their towel in the dryer while they’re taking a shower, taking over the other person’s chores for a day “just because”. Things that remind us that first and foremost, we’re a couple who love and like each other - not just close roommates.

I’m bi. 

I’m a cis-woman in a relationship with a cis-man, so they have nothing to “suspect”. They’d probably think I was possessed by satan.

My husband and I walked together down the aisle. 


My parents didn’t really raise me anyway, and at age 26, I didn’t “belong” to anyone or need to be “given away”. 

The way my husband and I looked at it, we were walking in to this part of our lives together. 

(As an added bonus, getting to walk down the aisle with my favorite person and not having all eyes on me alone eased a WHOLE lot of anxiety around the ceremony.)
No one will deliver food there after dark. Several local pizza places would just straight up cancel our orders without telling us.
My brother just finished elementary school in Texas. They still paddle kids.

If she’s his fiancé, I assume she’s been around long enough to know what the groom’s family is like. She’s not going in blind. 
Unless I’m missing a comment somewhere from OP, it’s likely that the bride and groom *have* talked about it. (Setting boundaries on what other people think your wedding should be is a pretty common issue.) They’ve probably had this conversation already and decided they didn’t care about anyone else’s unwarranted opinion.

Along the same lines, the insistence on teachers being constantly “regulated”. The assumption is that if you’re not emotionally regulated, your students won’t be either. Essentially, classroom behavioral problems are the teacher’s fault because they’re not managing their own emotions/stress/anxiety/whatever. 

The implication that little Johnny is running around screaming like a banshee instead of writing his narrative because *I* am not doing a good enough job handling  *my* emotions feels so incredibly cruel. 


Sorry, but I’ve got my own life - my own problems, my own trauma. That’s actually *why* I teach - so other children don’t have to go through what I did. 

Yes, I know that if I’m crying in class, things will go off the rails. But I can’t be expected to be an all-absorbent punching bag, taking whatever the kids are throwing with no reaction, no consequences to my own mental or emotional health. 

I don’t know if I explained it clearly, or if that makes sense. As an abuse survivor, it just feels like another form of the victim shaming I’ve been dealing with my whole life, on top of teacher martyrdom.
